title: The Loss of Friends (Frame - Pingalaka and Sanjivaka)
full_text:
In the southern city of Mahilaropya, there lived a wealthy and enterprising merchant named Vardhamanaka. Observing that even abundant gold diminishes when spent without being increased, he loaded two sturdy bullocks, named Sanjivaka and Nandaka, with rich merchandise and set out on the highway toward Kashmir to trade. As the heavy caravan wound through the dense, tangled jungle of the Vindhya mountains, Sanjivaka stumbled in a muddy ravine, fractured his fetlock, and collapsed in agony beneath the yoke.

Vardhamanaka wept over his faithful beast, but because the forest swarmed with tigers and leopards, his drivers urged him to press forward. Leaving hired men with grass and water to guard the bull, the merchant promised to return. Yet the frightened servants soon abandoned the bull and fled after the caravan, lying to their master that Sanjivaka had died.

Left alone in the wilderness, Sanjivaka did not despair. Licking his wounds, he cropped the luscious emerald grass near the sacred Yamuna river, drank the cool sweet water of mountain brooks, and slowly regained his strength. Within months, he grew as massive and sleek as a mountain cloud, his sharp horns polished like obsidian, and in the sheer joy of vigor, he would paw the earth and bellow with a roar that echoed through the hills like thunder.

Now in that same forest ruled a fierce and mighty lion named Pingalaka, sovereign of all four-footed beasts. Accompanied by his fierce retinue, Pingalaka went down to the river to drink, when suddenly Sanjivaka's thunderous bellow reverberated across the water. Having never heard the bellowing of a bull in the wild, the lion was seized with terror, suspecting that some colossal and supernatural creature had entered his realm. Concealing his dread, Pingalaka crouched beneath a banyan tree, refusing to hunt or stir.

Among the lion's courtiers were two discarded, impoverished jackals named Damanaka and Karataka, sons of the king's former prime minister. Observing their monarch's uneasy posture, Damanaka, who burned with ambitious cunning, whispered to Karataka: 'Look at our royal master! He sits paralyzed with fear, having forsaken the hunt. Let us discover the cause of his dread; by dispelling his terror, we shall regain our lost standing at court.'

Karataka cautioned his brother: 'Why interfere in affairs that do not concern us? He who meddles in business not his own comes to grief, like the monkey who pulled the wedge!'

Yet Damanaka refused to listen. Approaching Pingalaka with humble prostrations, he won the lion's confidence and learned of the mysterious bellow. Boldly offering to investigate, Damanaka trotted into the forest and encountered Sanjivaka. With honeyed words, the cunning jackal convinced the noble bull that King Pingalaka was a just and generous sovereign who desired his friendship. Bringing Sanjivaka to the court under a solemn pledge of safety, Damanaka introduced the two.

Upon meeting, Pingalaka and Sanjivaka recognized each other's noble nature and formed an intimate alliance. Day and night, the lion listened to the bull's profound discourses on statecraft, philosophy, and ethics, neglecting his carnivorous retinue and refusing to kill prey.

Seeing themselves starved and ignored, Damanaka's cunning turned to malice. Resolving to sunder their affection, he began whispering poison into Pingalaka's ear, claiming that Sanjivaka secretly conspired to usurp the throne, while simultaneously warning Sanjivaka that Pingalaka hungered for bull's flesh. Through deceitful slanders, the villainous jackal incited both friends to mortal combat, ending in the tragic death of the innocent Sanjivaka. As Vishnu Sharma warned:
"Even the firmest friendship that was forged with vows of gold
Will shatter into pieces when malicious tales are told;
A whisper in a jealous ear turns brother against brother,
Until the dearest companions destroy and slay each other."
moral: A friendship formed without prudence can easily be poisoned by wicked counselors who seek their own profit.

title: The Wedge-Pulling Monkey
full_text:
In the outskirts of a flourishing town, a wealthy merchant began the construction of an expansive temple dedicated to the welfare of travelers. Skilled carpenters, sawyers, and masons worked daily upon the site, hewing giant trunks of sal and teak into pillars, beams, and decorative cornices.

One sweltering noon, the master woodcutters were sawing halfway through a colossal timber log. To prevent the heavy cleft from snapping shut and binding the iron saw blade while they went to the nearby grove to eat their midday meal of rice and curds, the chief carpenter drove a stout, tapered wedge of khadira wood firmly into the open split.

Shortly after the workmen departed, a troop of wild, mischievous monkeys that inhabited the temple groves swung down from the branches to explore the abandoned construction site. They leaped upon the scaffolding, overturned baskets of lime, and rolled the iron chisels across the flagstones.

Among them was a young, reckless, and intensely curious monkey who could never let anything rest. Seeing the immense split log lying upon the ground, he hopped onto it, straddling the timber right over the open seam. His eyes fastened upon the wooden wedge projecting between the two halves.

'What a strange peg!' chattered the foolish creature. 'Why did those two-legged builders hammer it so tightly between these logs? I must discover what happens when it is loosened!'

Ignoring the uneasy silence of the clearing and his companions' warnings, the meddlesome monkey gripped the stout wedge with both hands, bracing his feet against the timber. He pulled, wrenched, and tugged with all his might. The wedge creaked, loosened slightly, and gave way.

In that instant, the enormous tension of the split log released with the force of an iron spring. The two massive halves slammed shut with a sickening thud, trapping the wretched monkey by his tail and legs. He shrieked in agony, unable to free himself, and perished miserably before the carpenters returned from their meal.

Relating this tale to his ambitious brother Damanaka, the wise jackal Karataka observed:
"He who thrusts his hand into a cleft he did not make,
And meddles in another's work for idle curiosity's sake,
Shall find the trap spring shut upon his folly and his pride,
Like the reckless forest monkey who pulled the wedge and died."
moral: He who meddles in affairs that do not concern him invites swift and certain disaster.

title: The Jackal and the War-Drum
full_text:
A famished jackal named Gomukha wandered across a barren plateau in search of food. His ribs showed through his matted hide, and his tongue hung parched from his jaws. As twilight gathered, he stumbled upon an old, abandoned battlefield where an army had encamped weeks before.

Suddenly, a deep, booming roar echoed through the thickets: 'DUM-DUM-DUM!' The hollow, menacing sound reverberated against the rocks like the footsteps of a colossal monster.

Gomukha's heart leaped into his throat. He tucked his tail between his trembling legs and turned to flee, whimpering in terror: 'Alas! What gigantic demon dwells in this wasteland? If I stay, he will swallow me in a single gulp!'

Yet as he took three panicked bounds, his natural cunning halted him. 'A brave soul,' thought the jackal, 'does not abandon his ground without discovering the truth. Let me examine the source of this frightful thunder before I surrender my hunting ground.'

Crawling cautiously on his belly through the tall, dry grass, Gomukha crept toward the sound. Parting the thorny bushes with his nose, he beheld a large military war-drum, discarded by soldiers beneath an overhanging creepers-laden banyan tree. Whenever the wind blew strong gusts across the ridge, the hanging wild vines whipped across the taut leather drumhead, producing the deep, resonant booming that shook the valley.

Realizing that the monster was nothing more than hollow wood and stretched cowhide, Gomukha chuckled at his foolish terror. He trotted boldly to the drum and thought: 'Surely an instrument that bellows with such an enormous voice must be filled with rich fat and succulent meat!'

He gnawed eagerly through the tough rawhide skin and squeezed his head inside the cavity. To his disappointment, he found nothing within except hollow air and dry wooden ribs. Yet his courage had conquered panic, and wandering nearby, he discovered carcasses left behind by the army, feasting till dawn.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"A hollow voice that shakes the hill may hide an empty frame;
The wise investigate the sound before they shrink in shame;
For he who flees a phantom noise before the truth is known
Surrenders fortune to the wind and starves in fear alone."
moral: Do not be terrified by loud sounds; investigate the source before you run in fear.

title: Merchant Strong-Tooth
full_text:
In the city of Vardhamana, there dwelt a wealthy and honorable merchant named Dantila, known far and wide as Strong-Tooth. Because of his exceptional honesty, civic generosity, and financial acumen, he was appointed chief superintendent of the city and enjoyed the unbounded favor and affection of the King. He was held in such high esteem that neither the nobles nor the royal family undertook any major enterprise without his counsel.

To celebrate his daughter's marriage, Dantila hosted a magnificent banquet at his mansion, inviting the King, the royal ministers, the priesthood, and all the city officials, showering each guest with costly gifts of silk, pearls, and sandalwood.

Among the crowd was Gorambha, a lowly sweeper whose duty was to sweep the royal bedchamber. Seeking to appear important, Gorambha took a seat upon an ornate cushioned divan reserved for high ministers of state. Seeing the insolent sweeper occupying the bench of dignitaries, Dantila was offended. He seized Gorambha by the collar, reprimanded him sharply before the assembled guests, and ordered the doorkeepers to thrust him out into the street.

Humiliated and burning with vengeance, Gorambha slunk away, muttering: 'You have shamed me publicly, Dantila! Though I am but a humble sweeper, you shall soon learn that even a fly can deposit poison in the ear of a king!'

A few days later, while sweeping the floor of the King's bedchamber at dawn, observing that the monarch was only half-awake, Gorambha pretended to mutter in an absentminded daze: 'How arrogant is merchant Dantila! He dares to embrace the Queen in the privacy of the palace garden, as if he were master of the realm!'

Hearing these words, the King bolted upright on his couch, his eyes blazing with fury. 'What did you say, Gorambha?' he roared. 'Is Dantila embracing the Queen?'

The sweeper threw himself upon the floor, trembling with feigned fright: 'Forgive me, Your Majesty! I was up all night gambling, and my mind was clouded with sleep. I know not what foolish babble escaped my lips!'

Suspicion, once planted in the heart of a monarch, spreads like wildfire. The King reasoned: 'A servant who sweeps my private chambers sees and hears what others cannot. Dantila has grown too powerful and familiar.'

Without investigating the slander, the King abruptly stripped Dantila of his honors, banished him from court, and forbade the palace guards to let him cross the gates. Bewildered and crushed by disgrace, Dantila retired to his house, unable to fathom how he had lost the royal favor.

A month later, as Dantila was walking down a narrow street, Gorambha passed him, sweeping the dust. Seeing the fallen merchant, the sweeper sneered: 'Beware, Dantila! Do not push past me, or I will have you driven out of this street as you had me driven from your wedding feast!'

In a flash of insight, Dantila understood the whole intrigue: 'This lowly sweeper whom I insulted has poisoned the King's mind!'

Swallowing his pride, Dantila invited Gorambha to his home that very evening, clothed him in fine garments, fed him savory sweets, and placed a purse of gold in his hands, apologizing with genuine courtesy for his past harshness. Delighted by the gifts, Gorambha promised to repair the damage.

Next morning, sweeping beside the King's couch, Gorambha muttered again: 'Our mighty King is so strange! He sits in the courtyard eating raw cucumbers while taking his morning bath!'

The King sprang up in anger: 'Insolent wretch! When did I ever eat cucumbers in my bath?'

'Pardon, Sire!' wept the sweeper. 'I am half-asleep and utter meaningless nonsense!'

The King reflected: 'If this fool babbles that I eat cucumbers in my bath, his babble about Dantila and the Queen was equally baseless!'

The King immediately summoned Dantila, restored all his honors, and appointed him chief minister, having learned that a ruler must never credit the unverified whispers of menials.
moral: Never insult or humiliate the humble servants of a king, for a slighted servant can bring down the mightiest counselor.

title: Godly and June
full_text:
In a tranquil hermitage on the banks of the sacred river Godavari lived a pious ascetic named Devasarman, known to the villagers as Godly. Through years of austerity, performing religious rituals, and receiving pious offerings from wealthy pilgrims, he had accumulated a fortune in pure gold coins. Trusting no bank, disciple, or relative, the ascetic sewed his gold into a heavy leather pouch, which he kept tied securely under his armpit day and night, guarding it as dearly as his own life.

In the neighboring town dwelt a cunning rogue and swindler named Ashadhaka, or June. Having watched the ascetic clutching his armpit wherever he walked, the swindler deduced that the holy man carried great wealth. June resolved to possess the treasure.

Approaching the hermitage with humble demeanor, barefoot and dressed in coarse bark garments, June prostrated himself before Godly, shedding tears of feigned devotion: 'Revered master! The illusions of this transient world have filled my heart with disgust. Accept me as your humblest disciple, let me wash your sacred feet, sweep your hermitage, and guide me upon the path of liberation!'

Flattered by the youth's eloquence, Godly accepted him as a novice. For many months, June served the ascetic with extraordinary diligence. He massaged the old man's weary feet, fetched firewood, cooked fragrant rice porridge, and never uttered a word of complaint. Yet despite June's devoted service, Godly never removed the leather pouch from his armpit, refusing to let the novice touch it even while bathing.

June thought bitterly: 'This old miser guards his gold like a serpent guarding its treasure. I must devise an irresistible distraction.'

One morning, the ascetic was invited by a wealthy disciple in an adjoining village to perform an initiation ceremony. Godly set out along the dusty road, accompanied by June, who carried his master's prayer mat and water pot.

Reaching the banks of a river, they saw two fierce mountain rams engaged in a violent duel, butting their curled horns together with bone-shattering crashes. Between the two fighting beasts hopped a foolish jackal, greedy to lap the blood that dripped from their bruised brows. Engrossed in the spectacle, the jackal failed to notice the rams backing up to charge; the two beasts collided at full speed, crushing the meddlesome jackal instantly.

Seeing the dead jackal, Godly paused to philosophize on the foolishness of greed. Taking advantage of his master's distraction, June pointed to a thicket and whispered: 'Revered master! While you perform your ablutions in the river, allow me to hold your holy cloak and prayer mat.'

Godly removed his outer robe, and feeling a sudden call of nature, he placed his precious leather pouch inside the folded cloak and stepped behind a cluster of reeds, ordering June to watch the garments carefully.

The instant the holy man disappeared behind the bushes, June snatched the leather pouch, stuffed it into his loincloth, and sprinted across the rocky ravine like a hunted deer.

When Godly emerged from the reeds, he found his prayer mat discarded upon the grass, the leather pouch gone, and the faithful disciple nowhere to be seen. He ran through the thickets, shouting June's name, weeping and tearing his matted hair in despair, but the rogue had vanished forever with the fruits of his lifetime.

Thus Vishnu Sharma warned:
"He who surrenders his treasure upon the word of a flattering knave,
Believing outer piety and vows of a servant slave,
Shall weep in bitter sorrow when the thief has fled the land,
Holding only empty tears within an empty hand."
moral: Never trust a flatterer whose sudden devotion masks a design upon your wealth.

title: The Jackal at the Ram-Fight
full_text:
In a rocky mountain meadow fringed with stunted pines, two powerful, thick-horned mountain rams were locked in a furious duel over the leadership of their flock. Backing away from each other for thirty paces, snorting steam into the chill air, they lowered their heavy foreheads and charged with all their might, colliding with a crash that sounded like thunder rolling across the crags.

Again and again they clashed, until their brows were bruised and drops of dark crimson blood spattered upon the gray stones.

A wandering jackal, driven half-mad by days of starvation, smelled the fresh blood from a nearby ridge. Lured by the intoxicating scent of gore, he crept through the scree, salivating with greedy anticipation. 'What a magnificent feast!' thought the scavenger. 'While these two stupid beasts batter each other, I can lap up their sweet blood and snatch the shreds of flesh falling from their heads!'

Blinded by his voracious appetite, the jackal ignored the violent momentum of the combatants. Instead of waiting at a safe distance for one of the rams to fall, he darted directly into the narrow space between them, lowering his snout to lick the blood from the rocks.

At that very second, both rams backed up, gathered their colossal strength, and charged forward at blinding speed. Their curved, iron-hard horns slammed together in the middle with bone-crushing fury, trapping the foolish jackal squarely between their brows.

With a single sickening impact, every bone in the scavenger's body was shattered, and he was flattened lifeless upon the bloody stones.

Thus Karataka instructed Damanaka on the perils of thrusting oneself between monarchs:
"Between two mighty forces engaged in mortal strife,
The greedy fool who enters pays the forfeit of his life;
Seek not the drops of profit where giants clash in wrath,
Lest their colliding fury crush your bones along the path."
moral: He who thrusts himself between two clashing forces in the hope of petty gain is crushed without mercy.

title: The Weaver's Wife
full_text:
In a prosperous manufacturing town lived an honest weaver named Mantharaka, who labored at his loom from dawn till dark, weaving fine silks for merchants. Though he was gentle and hardworking, his wife was vain, deceptive, and secretly unfaithful, spending her afternoons entertaining lovers while her husband worked.

One evening, having consumed a pot of strong palm liquor, the weaver returned home earlier than usual. As he approached his door, he saw a handsome young townsman slipping quietly out of his garden gate. Enraged by jealousy and alcohol, the weaver burst into the house, seized his wife by her hair, beat her with a wooden shuttle, and dragged her into the courtyard. Tying her securely to a stout wooden pillar, he shouted: 'Stay here tonight, wretched woman, and reflect upon your deceit!' Locking the outer gate, the drunken weaver threw himself upon his cot and fell into a stupor.

Shortly after midnight, the wife's confidante, an old barber's wife who lived next door, climbed over the garden wall. 'Your lover waits for you by the tamarind grove,' whispered the neighbor. 'Untie this cord and hasten to him; I will take your place tied to the post until you return.'

The unfaithful wife agreed eagerly. Untying the knots, she bound the barber's wife securely to the pillar and ran off into the night.

Presently, the weaver woke with a dry throat. Stumbling into the courtyard, he shouted angrily at the figure tied to the post: 'Are you ready to confess your guilt and beg for mercy?'

Fearing that her voice would reveal she was not his wife, the barber's wife remained completely silent.

Enraged by what he took for defiant stubbornness, the drunken weaver drew his sharp cobbler's knife, sliced off the tip of the woman's nose, and snarled: 'Now carry that ornament to your lovers!' Stumbling back into the bedroom, he resumed his snoring.

Before dawn, the weaver's wife returned. Finding the barber's wife mutilated and weeping in agony, she hurriedly untied her, bound herself back to the pillar, and sent the neighbor home with the severed piece of her nose.

As dawn broke, the weaver came out to gloat over his handiwork. In an instant, the cunning wife raised her hands to heaven and cried aloud in a pious voice: 'O all-seeing Sun and sacred Earth! If I have ever been unfaithful to my husband in thought, word, or deed, let my disfigurement remain forever! But if I am a chaste, pure, and blameless wife, let my severed nose be restored whole and beautiful this very instant!'

The weaver approached with a torch, and to his utter astonishment, beheld his wife's nose perfectly whole and untouched! Convinced that a divine miracle had vindicated her innocence, the foolish husband threw himself at her feet, wept bitter tears of remorse, and begged her forgiveness, pampering her with silks for the rest of his days.

Meanwhile, the barber's wife returned home clutching her bleeding face. When her husband, the barber, awoke and demanded his razor kit to attend to the town magistrate, she delayed handing it to him. Angered by her slowness, the barber threw a stray razor toward her feet. The cunning woman immediately fell to the floor, screaming: 'Murder! My husband has cut off my nose with his razor!'

The police arrested the bewildered barber and dragged him to the royal court, where the judge sentenced him to the gallows for maiming his wife. But just as the executioner readied the rope, an observant ascetic who had witnessed the whole midnight exchange stepped forward, revealed the severed nose found in the weaver's courtyard, and exposed the conspiracy. The barber was exonerated, while the deceitful women were condemned to public disgrace.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"A cunning tongue may weave a web of falsehood for a night,
And make the guilty seem adorned with virtue in the light;
Yet truth, like the unyielding dawn, breaks through the darkest shroud,
And casts the scheming hypocrite beneath the scornful crowd."
moral: Deceit and false vows lead to shame; the innocent who abets wickedness shares in its ruin.

title: How the Crow-Hen defeated the Black Snake
full_text:
In the spreading branches of a majestic banyan tree on the outskirts of an ancient city, a devoted pair of crows, Swift-Flight and his mate, built their woven nest. For several seasons they lived in peace, but a monstrous black cobra of enormous length made his dark burrow in the hollow trunk at the roots of that very tree.

Whenever the crow-hen laid her clutch of eggs and the fledglings hatched, the venomous serpent crawled up the hollow trunk, thrust his hooded head into the nest, and devoured the helpless chicks, leaving only broken shells and feathers. Year after year, the crows returned from foraging to find their nest empty, weeping bitter tears of grief.

At last, heartbroken and desperate, the crow-hen said to her mate: 'Beloved husband, we can endure this agony no longer. Let us abandon our ancestral tree and seek refuge in distant mountains, for who can dwell in peace with death coiled at the threshold?'

Swift-Flight replied: 'We have nested in this banyan for generations, and I will not be driven away by an insolent reptile. What we lack in physical strength, we must supply through intellect. Let us consult our wise friend, the jackal who lives in the neighboring ravine.'

Flying to the jackal's den, they recounted their sorrow. The jackal smiled shrewdly: 'Grieve no more, friends. The black snake is powerful and deadly, but he is completely devoid of cunning. You need not fight him with beak and claw; use the mighty arm of the king to crush him!'

'How can simple crows employ the king's arm?' asked Swift-Flight.

The jackal instructed them: 'Fly to the pleasure lake where the Prince and the ladies of the royal court bathe every afternoon. When the Prince removes his golden necklace studded with rubies and lays it upon the stone terrace, seize the jewel in your beak. Fly slowly, low enough that the royal guards can pursue you, and drop the necklace directly into the cobra's hollow burrow. The guards will do the rest.'

Next afternoon, Swift-Flight flew to the royal pavilion. Seeing the Prince swimming in the lotus pool with his attendants, the crow swooped down, grasped the dazzling ruby necklace in his beak, and flew off with a loud caw.

'Thief! A crow has stolen the Prince's necklace!' shouted the royal guards, drawing their swords and spears and racing after the bird.

Swift-Flight flew deliberately from tree to tree, ensuring the shouting soldiers never lost sight of the sparkling jewel. Reaching the banyan tree, he circled the branches and dropped the heavy necklace straight down into the black snake's hollow lair.

The royal guards arrived out of breath, surrounded the tree, and peered into the dark cavity with torches. As a soldier reached with a spear to retrieve the jewels, the disturbed black cobra reared up, expanding his hood and hissing with deadly fury.

'A venomous monster guards the stolen treasure!' cried the guards. With iron-tipped pikes and heavy clubs, they battered the cobra to death, pulled the ruby necklace from the hole, and returned in triumph to the palace.

Perched safely in the high branches above, Swift-Flight and his mate watched their mortal enemy perish without lifting a single claw. For the rest of their long lives, they raised generation after generation of healthy fledglings in peace and joy.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The blackest snake that terrorizes all the woodland space,
Whose venomous and hooded wrath no creature dares to face,
Falls easily before the mind that plans a shrewd design,
And turns the monarch's iron blade to serve its purpose fine."
moral: What cannot be accomplished by brute strength can easily be achieved through clever strategy.

title: The Heron that Liked Crab-Meat
full_text:
By the shores of an expansive, reed-fringed lake dwelt an elderly heron named Kanka. With age, his feathers grew ragged, his eyes dimmed, and his legs trembled, so that he could no longer dart his beak into the water to catch the swift carp and minnows. Starving and desperate, he stood motionless on one foot by the water's edge, letting great tears roll down his long bill.

A shrewd old crab crawled out from beneath a flat stone and asked with concern: 'Uncle, why do you stand so sorrowful today, refusing to strike at the fish swimming past your toes?'

The hypocritical heron sighed heavily: 'Alas, nephew! My heart breaks for the fate of my friends in this lake. This morning, as I rested near the town gate, I overheard three fishermen discussing their plans. They said: "This lake is teeming with fish and crabs. As soon as we finish netting the lotus pool across the valley, we will bring our giant drag-nets here and drain this water, capturing every living creature!"'

The terrified crab hurried to spread the news among the fish, frogs, and water tortoises. In panic, the aquatic creatures swarmed around the heron, pleading: 'Uncle, you are our only hope! You have wings; tell us how we can be saved from the fishermen's nets!'

Kanka replied with feigned benevolence: 'I am old and weak, but out of compassion, I will rescue you. Over the crest of that rocky ridge lies a hidden, spring-fed mountain pool, deep and secluded, where no fisherman's net can ever reach. If you trust me, I will carry you there one by one in my beak!'

The simple fish eagerly accepted his offer. Every morning, the heron took a fat fish in his bill, flew over the rocky ridge to a high granite slab, and there devoured the helpless creature, leaving only a heap of bleached white bones. For weeks, the treacherous bird feasted without effort, growing plump and sleek.

At last, the old crab approached him: 'Uncle, you have saved all my fish brothers, but you have left me behind. Carry me to the mountain pool, or I will die of sorrow!'

The heron thought greedily: 'I have eaten fish every day until I am sick of them. Crab meat will be a delicious and tender change of diet!'

Snatching the crab behind the shell in his long bill, Kanka took to the sky. As they soared over the rocky ridge, the crab peered down, looking for the promised spring-fed pool. To his horror, he saw no water, but only a flat granite rock covered with the skeletons and skulls of hundreds of devoured fish.

The crab realized the terrible truth: 'This villainous bird has murdered all my friends, and now he intends to smash my shell upon these rocks and eat me!'

Knowing that panic meant instant death, the crab summoned all his strength and presence of mind. As the heron angled his wings to alight upon the slaughter-slab, the crab reached around with his two massive, iron-hard pincer claws and clamped them securely around the heron's slender neck, squeezing with all his might.

The startled heron gasped for breath, flapped his wings in frantic terror, and choked, but the crab's pincers gripped like a vise. Tighter and tighter the crab squeezed until the heron's windpipe snapped, and the treacherous bird tumbled lifeless to the ground.

Severing the dead villain's head, the crab crawled slowly back over the ridge, down the muddy bank, and slipped into the lake. He displayed the heron's head to the surviving creatures and revealed how treachery had been avenged, earning their eternal gratitude.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The hypocrite who spins a web of false compassion round,
And leads the trusting to their doom upon the slaughter ground,
Shall find a sharp and sudden claw seize fast his throat in turn,
And reap the bloody consequence of what his malice earned."
moral: He who devises treachery against the innocent eventually falls victim to his own deceit.

title: Numskull and the Rabbit
full_text:
In a vast and verdant jungle dwelt a ferocious, bloodthirsty lion named Bhasuraka, or Numskull. Possessing colossal muscles and razor-sharp claws, he slaughtered forest animals indiscriminately, killing deer, boars, and antelopes for mere amusement long after his belly was full. The jungle echoed day and night with the terrified cries of hunted beasts.

Seeing their numbers rapidly decimated, the surviving animals—jackals, deer, boars, and rabbits—assembled under the shade of a sacred banyan to devise a plan for mutual preservation. Selecting their elder representatives, they approached Bhasuraka's cave with humble prostrations.

'O mighty Sovereign of the Forest!' spoke the elder deer. 'Why do you slaughter all your subjects in wasteful fury? If you exterminate us, who will remain to call you King? We come with a humble petition: remain peacefully in your royal cavern, and we pledge that every single day at noon, one animal chosen by lot shall present itself at your threshold for your royal meal. Thus you shall be fed without the toil of hunting, and our species shall not perish from the earth.'

Numskull pondered the offer and roared: 'Very well! But mark this condition: if a plump beast does not arrive at my cave each day before the shadow falls across the rock, I will resume my slaughter and devour every living creature in the woods!'

For months, the compact was observed. Each day, an animal chosen by lot surrendered its life to preserve the rest.

At last, the fateful lot fell upon an old, diminutive hare named Manduka. The weeping hares bid him farewell, but Manduka resolved not to die meekly. 'Brute force without wisdom is nothing,' thought the clever rabbit. 'I will use this tyrant's own arrogance and rage to destroy him.'

Instead of hastening to the lion's cave, the rabbit ambled leisurely through the forest, stopping to nibble succulent green clover, drink cool dew from fern leaves, and rest beneath flowering bushes. The sun climbed to its zenith and began to descend toward the western hills.

Inside his cavern, Numskull paced the floor, his stomach growling with ravenous hunger. 'The midday hour has passed!' roared the beast, gnashing his fangs. 'The animals have mocked me! Tomorrow morning, I will scour every thicket and slaughter every creature in the forest!'

Just as twilight settled, the little hare hopped casually into the cave, bowing with exaggerated reverence.

Numskull glared down upon him with bloodshot eyes: 'Insolent mite! You are so tiny you will not make half a mouthful for my tooth, and yet you dare to keep me waiting until nightfall? Tell me why I should not tear you to ribbons before I exterminate your entire race?'

Manduka replied with trembling humility: 'Sire! The fault is neither mine nor that of the woodland animals. Five fat hares were dispatched this morning for your royal banquet. But on the highway, a colossal lion of terrifying stature leaped from an underground fortress and seized us! He roared: "Where are you taking these hares? This forest belongs to me, King Bhasuraka is an imposter and a thief, and I will devour anyone who honors him!"'

'I pleaded with him,' continued the rabbit, 'saying that we belonged to the true monarch. The stranger laughed and released me, commanding: "Run to that coward Bhasuraka, tell him to meet me at my fortress, and whichever lion proves stronger in battle shall rule the forest alone!" That, Sire, is why I am late.'

Numskull's vanity exploded into blind fury. His mane bristled and his roar shook the cavern walls: 'An imposter dares to claim my kingdom? Lead me to this insolent scoundrel immediately, and I will tear his heart from his ribs!'

'Follow me, Sire,' said the rabbit, hopping briskly through the woods.

He led the enraged tyrant to a secluded clearing where an ancient, deep stone well was filled to the brim with crystal-clear water. 'He hides in his water-fortress, Sire,' whispered the rabbit, pointing to the mossy rim. 'He saw you coming and retreated inside.'

Numskull leaped upon the stone coping and peered down into the depths. There, in the mirror-smooth surface of the dark water, he saw the perfect reflection of a colossal lion with bristling mane and blazing eyes, accompanied by a little hare!

Mistaking his own reflection for the rival monarch, Numskull unleashed a deafening roar of challenge: 'ROAAAR!'

The deep, echo-chamber of the stone cylinder magnified the roar and flung it back with terrifying force: 'ROAAAR!'

Believing the challenger was roaring back with double fury, Numskull lost all reason. Gathering his colossal hind legs, he hurled himself headlong into the deep well to tear his enemy apart. He struck the cold water, his heavy head cracked against the bottom stones, and he drowned in the dark depths.

The clever little rabbit hopped back to the banyan grove, singing with joy. The forest animals rejoiced, hailing the tiny hare as their savior, and lived forever in freedom and peace.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who possesses intellect possesses supreme might;
The physically strong who lacks all wit falls helpless in the fight;
Behold the monstrous Numskull who made the mountains shake,
Cast down to drown within a well by one diminutive hare."
moral: Intelligence is true strength; a diminutive creature with wit can destroy a ferocious tyrant.

title: The Weaver Who Loved a Princess
full_text:
In the northern capital of Pundravardhana lived two intimate companions: Kaulikaka, an artistic weaver of fine fabrics, and a brilliant master carpenter named Vishvamukha. During the spring carnival, as royal elephants paraded through the flower-strewn avenues, Kaulikaka looked up at the marble balcony of the royal palace and beheld the King's daughter, Princess Chandravati. Her beauty was like the full moon rising over lotuses, and in that single heartbeat, the humble weaver was struck by love so consuming that he fell upon the street in a swoon.

Carried home by his companion, the weaver took to his bed, refusing food and water. 'Friend,' wept Kaulikaka, 'I am a humble artisan, and she is the daughter of an emperor. Since my love can never be realized in this life, I must starve myself to death.'

The carpenter chided him: 'Despair is the companion of fools! True friends exist to achieve what seems impossible. Rise and eat, for I have devised a plan.'

Retiring to his workshop, the ingenious carpenter selected aromatic sandalwood, fine iron springs, and carved wooden levers, constructing a magnificent mechanical Garuda bird. Its wings were covered with feathers painted in brilliant azure, gold, and emerald; its head was adorned with a crest of pearls, and within its hollow belly was a seat with levers that allowed the rider to fly through the air, rise, dive, and alight with ease.

The carpenter brought the mechanical bird to his friend, along with a four-armed costume of luminous yellow silk, a shining diadem, a replica mace, and a sparkling lotus. 'Disguise yourself as the four-armed Lord of the Universe,' instructed the carpenter. 'Fly by night through the skies to the rooftop terrace of the princess's private apartments. When she beholds the divine Garuda alighting from heaven, she will receive you with reverence.'

That very midnight, Kaulikaka donned the celestial robes, mounted the mechanical bird, pulled the flight levers, and soared into the starlit sky. Guided by the moon, he hovered over the palace and landed gently upon the princess's marble terrace.

Waking from sleep, Princess Chandravati was dazzled by the celestial apparition. Falling to her knees, she stammered prayers, believing the Supreme Preserver had descended from the heavens. Kaulikaka addressed her with solemn dignity, explaining that because of her sublime virtues, he had chosen her for his consort in the Gandharva manner. The princess rejoiced, and night after night, the mechanical Garuda visited the terrace, bringing joy to the lovers.

Soon, observing that the princess bloomed with radiant happiness, the King questioned her. She revealed the secret visits of her divine husband. Astonished and proud, the King believed his dynasty was guarded by heaven itself. Becoming arrogant, he refused to pay tribute to the neighboring Emperor of Kalinga and treated foreign ambassadors with contempt.

Enraged, the Emperor of Kalinga invaded the realm with ten thousand war elephants, fifty thousand horsemen, and an ocean of foot soldiers. They besieged the capital, shattering the outer ramparts. The King climbed the terrace and prayed: 'O Divine Son-in-law! Save my kingdom from destruction!'

Hearing the King's despair and knowing the siege would destroy his beloved Chandravati, the humble weaver was gripped with agony of conscience. 'I have deceived this noble family,' thought Kaulikaka. 'If I flee on my wooden bird, I am a cowardly fraud. It is better to die fighting like a warrior in defense of the maiden I love than to live as an imposter.'

Mounting the mechanical Garuda at dawn, he soared high into the sky over the battlefield, brandishing his wooden mace and shouting battle cries, determined to plunge into the enemy ranks and sacrifice his life for the princess.

Observing from the celestial realms, the true Lord Narayana smiled upon the humble artisan. 'This mortal has assumed my divine form,' thought the Lord. 'If he falls before the Kalinga army, mortals will mock my holy name, saying that the Preserver was defeated by mortal archers. Moreover, his love is pure and his courage is steadfast.'

The divine spirit entered the mechanical bird and filled the weaver's arms with supernatural might. As the wooden Garuda swooped over the battlefield, blinding lightning flashed from its wings, thunder roared from the clear sky, and the enemy ranks fell into wild panic. The Emperor of Kalinga surrendered his crown and begged for peace.

Returning to the palace in glory, Kaulikaka landed before the King and Queen. Filled with honest humility, he dismounted, removed his diadem, and confessed the entire truth—his humble birth, the mechanical bird, and the deceit born of love.

Instead of anger, the King embraced him: 'He who possessed the courage to face an army alone for love, and upon whose valiant heart heaven bestowed its own power, is worthier than any prince!' The King formally bestowed Princess Chandravati's hand upon Kaulikaka in marriage and made him viceroy of the realm.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"A humble station cannot bind a soul of valiant grace;
When courage and fidelity illuminate the face,
Even the gods descend to bless the mortal who would die
To shield the honor of his love beneath the open sky."
moral: Even when one assumes a high disguise, true nobility of action alone wins honor and divine grace.

title: The Ungrateful Man
full_text:
In a quiet village near the Vindhya hills lived an impoverished, kind-hearted Priest named Yajnadatta. Traveling through the wilderness in search of employment, he came upon a deep, abandoned well whose masonry had collapsed. Hearing pitiful cries rising from the dark pit, the Priest leaned over the stone rim and peered down.

Trapped at the muddy bottom were four miserable creatures: a fierce tiger, an ape, a venomous black cobra, and a man dressed in fine merchant's robes.

Seeing the holy man, the tiger pleaded: 'O compassionate Priest, throw down a rope and rescue me! I swear by the sacred mountains that I will never harm you, but will repay your kindness!'

Yajnadatta hesitated, fearing the predator's claws, but pity moved his heart. Lowering a strong vine rope, he hauled the heavy tiger to safety. The tiger bowed low and said: 'I dwell in the cavern of the southern ridge. If you ever pass that way and need food, visit my cave.'

The Priest lowered the vine again and pulled up the ape. The ape chattered gratefully: 'I live in the wild mango grove on the cliff. Whenever you hunger, come, and I will shake down sweet fruits for you.'

Next, the black cobra called from the mud: 'Rescue me also, O gentle sage! Though my bite is death to the wicked, I will never harm my savior. If ever you find yourself in mortal danger, remember me, and I will come to your aid.' The Priest pulled up the serpent, who thanked him and slithered into the grass.

As the Priest prepared to depart, the four creatures warned him in unison: 'Revered master, leave the fourth prisoner in the pit! Do not rescue that man. Humans are deceitful, treacherous, and ungrateful; if you save him, he will repay your kindness with ruin.'

Yet the tender-hearted Priest thought: 'He is a fellow human being; how can I leave him to starve in a dark hole?' He lowered the vine a fourth time and hauled the man out of the well.

The rescued man prostrated himself, saying: 'I am Suvarnakara, a master goldsmith in the capital city of Ujjayini. If you ever visit the city and have gold or silver to work, come to my shop, and I will serve you with all my skill.'

Months passed, and extreme poverty struck the Priest's household. Remembering the promises, Yajnadatta journeyed into the forest. He visited the ape, who joyfully filled his basket with delicious wild mangoes, figs, and honey. He then visited the tiger's cave; the noble beast welcomed him, bowed his head, and laid at his feet a magnificent golden necklace and jeweled ornaments (which the tiger had taken from a prince who had fallen from his horse in the forest).

Delighted, the Priest thought: 'These ornaments will banish my poverty forever! I will take them to the goldsmith whom I rescued; he will melt them down honestly and pay me their true value in silver.'

Entering the goldsmith's shop in Ujjayini, Yajnadatta presented the jewels. The greedy artisan immediately recognized the necklace: it belonged to the King's son, who had recently disappeared in the forest!

Instead of gratitude, dark ambition seized the goldsmith: 'If I surrender this beggar to the King as the prince's murderer, the King will reward me with immense riches and royal favor!'

Ordering the Priest to rest while he evaluated the gold, the treacherous goldsmith ran straight to the royal palace and informed the King that the prince's assassin was in his shop. Royal guards seized the bewildered Priest, bound him in heavy chains, and cast him into the deepest dungeon, sentenced to be impaled upon the stake at dawn.

Sitting in the cold, rat-infested cell, the weeping Priest remembered the warning of the beasts: 'Alas! The tiger, the ape, and the cobra spoke the truth. The human alone was devoid of honor.'

Remembering the cobra's promise, he called the serpent in his heart. Instantly, the black cobra slipped through the dungeon bars and coiled at his feet: 'What is your command, my savior?'

The Priest recounted the goldsmith's betrayal. The cobra said: 'I will avenge you tonight. I will enter the palace bedchamber and bite the King's beloved daughter, the Princess. My venom will resist all physicians, charms, and herbs. No medicine in creation can cure her except the touch of your hand upon her forehead. When the King proclaims that anyone who cures the princess will receive half the kingdom, step forward, touch her brow, and reveal the truth.'

That night, the princess was bitten. The court physicians, sorcerers, and snake-charmers were helpless; the maiden lay cold and breathless on her couch. Proclamations were shouted through the city promising wealth and honors to whoever could neutralize the venom.

The Priest informed the dungeon warden that he could cure the princess. Led to the royal bedchamber, Yajnadatta placed his hand upon the maiden's forehead. At his touch, the miraculous venom dissolved; color returned to her cheeks, and she opened her eyes in perfect health!

Overjoyed, the King embraced the Priest and asked how he possessed such power. Yajnadatta revealed the entire history—the deep well, the gratitude of the tiger, ape, and snake, the betrayal of the goldsmith, and the true source of the prince's necklace.

The King's wrath fell upon the treacherous artisan. He ordered the ungrateful goldsmith impaled upon the stake, while Yajnadatta was granted a thousand fertile villages, high ministerial office, and lived in honor, proving forever:
"Wild beasts of fang and claw remember kindness well,
And return loyalty from the forest where they dwell;
But the false heart of man turns venomous and cold,
And sells his savior's life for petty crumbs of gold."
moral: Wild beasts remember kindness and return loyalty; but a deceitful, ungrateful human knows no honor.

title: Leap and Creep
full_text:
In the opulent bedchamber of a wealthy King stood a magnificent royal bedstead of carved teak, adorned with embroidered silks and covered with a mattress of softest eiderdown as white as the foam of the ocean. Within the dark, secluded folds of this royal mattress lived a discreet and well-mannered louse named Mandavisarpini, or Creep.

For many years, Creep had raised her family in comfort. She observed the strictest domestic prudence: she waited until the King had fallen into a deep, heavy slumber, and only then would she crawl forth with gentle, microscopic feet, drink a single, tiny drop of royal blood, and slip back into her fold without causing the slightest irritation or itch. Because of her restraint, her presence was never suspected, and she lived in peace.

One evening, an energetic, voracious, and reckless flea named Tiktamukha, or Leap, blown by the wind through the open palace windows, hopped into the royal bedchamber and landed squarely upon the eiderdown mattress.

Seeing the stranger, Creep hurried out of her fold: 'Who are you, stranger? This bed belongs to the King, and my family dwells here under strict discipline. Depart immediately, for your erratic leaping will bring discovery!'

Leap bowed with hypocritical humility: 'Sister! I am a wandering mendicant. I have tasted the coarse, bitter blood of beggars, soldiers, and cattle, but never in all my travels have I tasted the sweet, perfumed blood of a monarch nourished on almonds, saffron, and rich delicacies! As a guest at your threshold, grant me one tiny taste of royal blood, and I will depart at dawn singing your praises!'

Creep hesitated, swayed by the sacred duty of hospitality, but warned: 'Very well, brother, you may drink. But mark this rule: you must wait until the King is soundly asleep, snoring peacefully with all his limbs relaxed. Then you may sip gently without biting or causing pain.'

Leap promised with solemn vows, but patience was entirely foreign to his reckless nature.

No sooner had the King lain down upon his couch, before his eyes were even closed or his breathing slowed, than the ravenous flea hopped onto his neck and plunged his sharp beak deep into the tender flesh, biting with voracious greed!

The King started up in bed with a sharp cry: 'Ho, chamberlains! A stinging insect has bitten me upon my neck! Light the torches and examine the mattress!'

Hearing the commotion, the agile flea sprang into the air, leaped across the bedposts, and slipped safely into a narrow crack in the floorboards.

The royal servants rushed into the bedchamber with torches, stripped off the sheets, and searched the folds of the mattress. Unable to catch the leaping flea, their eyes fell upon the slow, harmless louse Creep, crawling quietly among the seams.

'Here is the villainous creature that bit Your Majesty!' shouted the servants, and with a single squeeze of their fingers, poor Creep and her innocent children were crushed to death.

Thus Vishnu Sharma warned:
"He who invites a reckless rogue to share his quiet nest,
Believing honeyed promises spoken by a greedy guest,
Shall see the scoundrel flee the storm when sudden perils wake,
While innocence pays the forfeit for another's reckless sake."
moral: Do not harbor an untrustworthy companion whose reckless greed brings ruin upon your quiet home.

title: The Blue Jackal
full_text:
A mangy, cowardly jackal named Chandarava roamed the outskirts of a flourishing town in search of garbage to fill his hollow belly. Wandering into the streets after midnight, he was spotted by a pack of fierce, barking street dogs. Yelping in chorus, the ferocious mastiffs chased the terrified scavenger down winding alleys, biting his hind legs and tearing his ears.

Desperate to save his life, Chandarava darted through the open doorway of a dyer's courtyard. In his panicked haste, he slipped on the wet flagstones and plunged headlong into an enormous wooden vat filled to the brim with dark blue indigo dye!

He submerged completely, holding his breath until the barking dogs lost his scent and trotted away down the lane. Crawling out of the vat, dripping wet and shivering, the jackal slunk into the forest under the cover of darkness.

When dawn broke and the morning sun shone through the trees, Chandarava looked down at his reflection in a quiet pool. He gasped in astonishment: from the tip of his nose to the hairs of his tail, his coat had turned a brilliant, luminous, celestial sapphire blue! Not a single speck of his dirty yellow fur remained visible.

As he walked through the forest clearing, the sight of this extraordinary creature stunned the beasts. Tigers, leopards, lions, bears, and elephants stared in awe and backed away in terror, whispering among themselves: 'What miraculous being is this? His skin is the color of the midnight sky! We know neither his strength nor his origin; we must flee before he destroys us!'

Seeing the mighty predators trembling before him, Chandarava's cunning mind grasped the opportunity. Posing majestically upon a high rock, he called out in a resonant, solemn voice: 'Do not flee, O creatures of the forest! I am Kakudruma, created by the Lord of the Universe and sent down from heaven to be your supreme Sovereign! Seeing that the four-footed beasts were living without a king and falling into mutual strife, the gods anointed me with celestial blue nectar. Live peacefully under my royal umbrella, and I will protect you from all harm!'

Believing the divine tale, the mighty lion Pingalaka, the ferocious tiger, the leopard, and all the forest beasts bowed their heads to the earth, proclaiming Kakudruma their king.

The blue jackal established his court with regal pomp. He appointed the lion as his commander-in-chief, the tiger as lord chamberlain, and the leopard as minister of defense. But toward his own kinsmen—the poor jackals of the forest—he was ruthless. Fearing they might recognize him, he ordered them driven from the forest under penalty of death.

For many months, the imposter ruled in luxury. The lion and tiger hunted fat game and laid the choice meats before his throne, and Kakudruma feasted without lifting a paw, arrogant in his unearned glory.

One evening, as King Kakudruma sat upon his royal rock surrounded by his fierce predators, the full moon rose over the mountain ridges. From the distant plains beyond the trees, a pack of wild jackals began their evening chorus, lifting their muzzles and howling in long, mournful, high-pitched wails: 'Owoooo! Owoooo! Ahoo-ahoo!'

Hearing the ancestral cry of his own kind, Chandarava felt his heart flutter with uncontrollable excitement. The hair on his back bristled; his ancestral instinct conquered all caution, courtly manners, and prudence. Unable to restrain the call of his blood, the blue monarch tilted his head toward the moon, opened his jaws, and howled at the top of his lungs: 'OWOOOO! AHOO-AHOO-AHOOO!'

The lion, the tiger, and the leopard froze. They looked at each other in thunderous realization: 'He is no celestial sovereign sent from heaven! He is nothing more than a common, mangy jackal who painted himself blue!'

Realizing his fatal blunder, Chandarava turned to flee, but before he could take three bounds, the ferocious tiger sprang upon him with flashing claws, tearing the imposter to shreds on the spot.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Though you paint your skin with indigo and wear a monarch's crown,
And make the mighty beasts of prey before your foot bow down,
Your natural voice and instincts will your secret fraud betray,
And strip the borrowed majesty of false deceit away."
moral: An artificial disguise cannot conceal one's true nature; true character is revealed when the moment of instinct arrives.

title: Passion and the Owl
full_text:
In a rugged mountain valley stood an ancient, hollow silk-cotton tree inhabited by a large horned owl named Ratnamukha. In that same valley lived a handsome wild pigeon named Kamandaka, who spent his days fluttering among the flowering creepers, singing sweet coos of affection to his mate.

One stormy season, a cruel hawk struck down the female pigeon, leaving Kamandaka alone in the wilderness. Blinded by grief and unnatural passion, the foolish bird refused to seek a mate among his own kind. Flying past the hollow silk-cotton tree, he saw the yellow eyes of the horned owl glaring from the dark hollow and conceived a bizarre, uncontrollable affection for the nocturnal predator.

Alighting upon a branch before the hollow, the pigeon bowed and cooed with amorous verses, praising the owl's hooked beak, fierce talons, and nocturnal majesty.

The owl, who found the daytime light blinding and hated the chatter of day-birds, blinked his great round eyes and snapped: 'Foolish pigeon! You fly in the golden sun and feed on sweet grain, while I hunt rats in the pitch darkness of night. Our natures are completely opposed; fly away and leave me to sleep!'

Yet the infatuated pigeon refused to depart. Day after day, he perched before the hollow, singing love songs and neglecting his food, crying: 'Love knows no difference of species or habit! If you will not accept me, I will perish before your threshold!'

At last, as twilight fell and hunger gnawed at the owl's belly, the predator looked upon the plump, foolish bird that insisted on pressing itself into his claws.

'If you love me so dearly,' hissed the owl with a sinister chuckle, 'enter my dark hollow, and we shall be united forever!'

Rejoicing that his suit had triumphed, the foolish pigeon hopped eagerly into the dark cavity of the silk-cotton tree. In an instant, the owl clamped his razor talons around the pigeon's throat, tore off his feathers, and swallowed him whole, putting a swift end to his unnatural passion.

Thus Vishnu Sharma warned against foolish, mismatched associations:
"He who seeks love where nature set a chasm wide and deep,
Ignoring species, character, and habits that they keep,
Walks blind into the predator's unyielding, bloody lair,
And pays with life the forfeit of his foolish, blind affair."
moral: An unnatural union or foolish obsession leads only to ridicule, misery, and destruction.

title: Ugly's Trust Abused
full_text:
In an expansive wilderness lived a mighty lion named Madotkata, accompanied by three fawning, parasitic courtiers: a cunning crow named Chaturanana, a deceitful jackal named Mahachatura, and a ferocious leopard named Kravyamukha. The three companions survived entirely upon the scraps of meat left behind by the lion after his kills.

One day, while roaming the edge of the forest, they came upon an unusual creature that had wandered away from a passing merchant's caravan: a tall, ungainly domestic camel named Kathanaka, or Ugly. The camel had an awkward gait, a long curved neck, and a drooping hump.

Brought before the lion, the camel prostrated himself and begged for protection. Madotkata, pleased by the strange beast's humility, granted him a solemn pledge of safety, saying: 'Fear nothing in this forest, brother. You have sought my royal refuge; graze freely upon the sweet acacia shoots, and no creature shall harm a hair of your hide.' For many months, the camel grazed peacefully, growing fat and sleek under the royal guarantee.

It happened that during a fierce battle with a rogue wild elephant, King Madotkata was severely wounded. His ribs were bruised, his paws were pierced by tusks, and he lay helpless in his cavern, unable to stalk prey or leap upon deer.

Days passed, and the three courtiers grew weak with starvation. The cunning crow whispered to the jackal: 'Our master starves, and we are famished corpses. Why should we look far for meat when this fat, useless camel grazes right outside the cave? Let us persuade the lion to kill him!'

The jackal objected: 'Our master gave the camel a solemn vow of safety; he will never break his royal oath.'

'Leave that to me,' sneered the crow. 'I will twist the situation so that the camel himself begs to be eaten!'

Entering the cave, the crow spoke to the starving lion: 'Sire, you are dying of hunger, and without your strength, we must all perish. Why not feast upon the camel?'

Madotkata roared with righteous anger: 'Shame upon you, villain! I gave him my word of safety when he sought my sanctuary! He who betrays a guest who trusted in his honor commits the blackest sin in creation!'

The crow bowed low: 'Sire, you speak with noble majesty. I would never ask you to break your oath. But what if the camel willingly and gladly offers his own body out of love and gratitude for his sovereign?'

The starving lion remained silent, and silence is the consent of weakness.

The crow assembled the three courtiers and the camel outside the cave. Entering together, the crow stepped forward, bowed to the ground, and said: 'Sire! You are our life and protector. Rather than watch you starve, take my humble body, devour my flesh, and restore your royal strength!'

The jackal interrupted: 'You are so small, crow, that your feathers would scarcely clean the king's teeth! Let our master devour me instead!'

The leopard stepped forward: 'You are a jackal, whose flesh is foul and tough! I am a sleek leopard; let our sovereign feast upon my tender meat!'

Hearing his three companions display such apparent nobility and self-sacrifice, the simple, honest camel was deeply moved. Trusting in the lion's solemn vow of protection, the camel thought: 'They have each offered their lives and been spared because of their unsuitability. Surely if I offer my large, plump body, the king will praise my gratitude and spare me likewise!'

The camel stepped forward, bowed his long neck, and spoke with pure sincerity: 'Sire! None of these companions have meat sufficient for your majesty. My body is large and nourished on sweet leaves; devour me and sustain your royal life!'

No sooner had the words left the camel's lips than the treacherous crow shrieked: 'Our noble brother offers himself freely! Hail his devotion!'

Before the bewildered camel could utter another word, the ravenous leopard leaped upon his back, the jackal tore open his throat, and the starving lion sank his fangs into his ribs, devouring the innocent beast who had trusted in their honor.

Thus Vishnu Sharma warned against trusting treacherous counselors:
"Wicked companions who surround the throne with flattering art
Will twist the royal promise and corrupt the monarch's heart;
Let no one trust the sacred pledge of refuge in that den
Where flatterers whisper malice in the ears of starving men."

title: The Lion and the Carpenter
full_text:
In a flourishing village near the forest lived an industrious, skilled carpenter named Somaka. One morning, he shouldered his heavy iron adze, saws, and measuring cords, heading into the woods to fell a sturdy sal tree for timber.

While he was inspecting a tall trunk, a ferocious wild lion bounded into the clearing, his eyes blazing like live coals, his mane bristling with murderous fury. 'Two-legged intruder!' roared the beast. 'You have entered my domain to steal my trees! Prepare to be torn to pieces!'

Somaka froze. He knew that flight was impossible, for the lion could run down a deer in seconds, and his light adze was useless against the predator's colossal jaws. He remembered that presence of mind is the only weapon when facing overwhelming force.

Instead of screaming or trembling, the carpenter bowed with polite, professional courtesy: 'Greetings, mighty Monarch of the Woods! I have not come to steal your trees; I have come at the urgent request of your royal council! The council has decided that since you are the supreme Sovereign of all beasts, you must possess a majestic, secure throne-box of aromatic wood, fitted with sliding bolts, wherein you can rest in royal majesty away from gnats, rain, and insolent hyenas!'

The vain lion paused, flattered by the prospect of a royal throne-box: 'Is it true? Where is this royal chamber?'

'I have just completed the framework!' replied the carpenter, pointing to a heavy, hollow timber crate he had built to store his iron tools. 'It is spacious, sturdy, and lined with smooth cedar. But before I deliver it to your courtiers, you must enter and test whether its dimensions suit your royal majesty.'

Curious and puffed up with vanity, the foolish lion stepped inside the narrow wooden box, curling his tail to fit inside.

'Does it feel comfortable, Sire?' asked the carpenter smoothly.

'It seems a trifle snug,' replied the lion from within.

'Allow me to test the sliding lid and the safety bolts,' said Somaka. With lightning speed, he slammed down the heavy oak lid, drove four iron pins through the mortises, and hammered the iron brackets tight with his mallet!

Trapped in the pitch darkness, unable to turn or extend his claws, the lion roared with fury, battering against the stout timber, but the seasoned wood held firm.

The carpenter shouldered his tools and laughed: 'Brute strength is a formidable gift, King of Beasts, but it is nothing compared to the intelligence of an artisan!' Leaving the trapped beast secured for the village hunters, the carpenter walked home in safety and peace.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The sharpest fangs and heaviest claws that strike the forest blind
Are helpless as a newborn babe before the thinking mind;
He who meets danger with a calm and calculating wit
Can trap the monarch of the woods within a wooden pit."
moral: Human wit and ingenuity can ensnare and conquer the most ferocious brute strength.

title: The Plover Who Fought the Ocean
full_text:
Upon the sandy shores of the great Eastern Ocean dwelt a pair of tiny titibha birds, or sand-plovers. When the breeding season arrived, the hen-plover, heavy with eggs, said to her mate: 'Beloved husband, let us seek a secluded nesting ground far inland among the mountain foothills, for when the full-moon tide swells, the mighty ocean will surge across these flats and wash our eggs away.'

The cock-plover, proud and spirited, puffed out his feathers: 'Do not fear, my love! Lay your eggs right here upon the white sands. I should like to see this arrogant Ocean dare to touch the offspring of a bird of my stature!'

The hen laughed at his boasting: 'How foolish you are! What comparison is there between a tiny plover and the colossal ocean whose waves swallow continents? He who ignores the counsel of prudent friends invites destruction.'

Yet to appease her mate, she laid her precious clutch of spotted eggs in a depression upon the high tide line.

The Ocean, who heard the tiny bird's arrogant words, was amused and offended. 'Look at this tiny creature!' rumbled the deep water. 'He dares to challenge my majesty. I will test his resolve!'

On the night of the full moon, as the parent birds flew along the shore to feed, the Ocean unleashed a colossal, frothing wave that swept over the sandbank, sucked the nest into the depths, and carried the eggs away into the abyss.

Returning at dawn to find the nest empty, the hen-plover wept in despair, tearing her feathers: 'Did I not warn you, husband? The cruel ocean has swallowed our children!'

The cock-plover stood tall upon the rocks, his eyes burning with unyielding determination: 'Dry your tears, wife! You shall behold the power of my resolve! I will dry up this arrogant ocean and force him to surrender our children, even if it takes a hundred lifetimes!'

Perching upon the water's edge, the tiny bird dipped his slender beak into the sea, sucked up a drop of salt water, flew to the dry sands, and shook the drop onto the earth. Back and forth he flew: one drop, two drops, three drops, determined to empty the colossal sea!

Watching him, the hen said: 'Husband, your beak cannot empty an ocean in ten thousand yugas! How can you succeed without powerful allies?'

The cock-plover immediately sounded the assembly call of all feathered creatures. Flocks of plovers, cranes, herons, gulls, and eagles darkened the sky, gathering around the determined father. Hearing of the Ocean's insolence, the assembled birds shouted in solidarity: 'An insult to one bird is an insult to all!'

Led by the noble eagle, the host of birds flew to the celestial mountain of Vaikuntha and petitioned the supreme Garuda, king of winged beings and mount of the Preserver. 'O mighty Garuda!' cried the birds. 'The Ocean, proud of his vast waters, has swallowed the offspring of our brother plover! If you permit such tyranny, no bird on earth will ever breed in peace!'

Garuda's wrath was kindled. Spreading his colossal wings that spanned three leagues, the celestial eagle flew to the shore, landing upon the cliffs like a falling mountain. He dipped his razor beak toward the waves and roared: 'Hear me, arrogant Ocean! Surrender the plover's eggs unharmed this very instant, or I will dry up your waters with the fiery wind of my wings, leaving you a desert of scorched sand!'

Terrified by the wrath of the celestial eagle, the Ocean trembled to his deepest trenches. The waters parted, and the Ocean personified emerged from the waves bearing a golden basin containing the plover's spotted eggs, unbroken and safe, laying them humbly at the tiny bird's feet and begging forgiveness for his arrogance.

The joyful plovers hatched their brood in triumph, surrounded by their loyal friends.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Though weak and diminutive your frame, if your resolve be high,
And loyal companions join your cause beneath the vaulted sky,
The proudest tyrant on the earth will bend his haughty crest,
And yield the treasure he had stolen back to the humble nest."
moral: Even the weakest creature, when united with steadfast friends and unwavering resolve, can conquer the mighty ocean.

title: Shell-Neck Slim and Grim
full_text:
In a tranquil lake nestled among the lotus-covered valleys of Magadha lived a water tortoise named Kambugriva, or Shell-Neck. For many peaceful years, he enjoyed the intimate, devoted friendship of two handsome wild geese, named Sankata and Vikata, or Slim and Grim. Every morning, the two winged companions flew down to the water's edge to converse with Shell-Neck on philosophy, the nature of seasons, and the joys of virtue.

A prolonged, severe drought struck the region. No rain fell from the brazen sky for three consecutive seasons; the mountain streams ceased flowing, the lotus leaves withered to dust, and the waters of the lake began to evaporate into foul, shallow mud.

Seeing their lake drying up, Slim and Grim said sorrowfully to their friend: 'Beloved Shell-Neck, the water has vanished and the mud burns like hot ashes. Soon this basin will be a desert of cracked earth. We have strong wings to fly across the mountain ridges to an expansive lake fed by Himalayan glaciers, but our hearts break to leave you behind to perish in the mud.'

Shell-Neck wept bitterly: 'You are my brothers! Water is your recreation, but it is my very life. Without water, I cannot survive three days. If you love me, devise some ingenious means to carry me with you!'

The two geese pondered deeply. Slim said: 'We have devised a plan, brother, but it requires unyielding discipline on your part. We will bring a stout, smooth wooden staff. You must bite firmly onto the middle of the staff with your jaws, holding it with all your strength. Grim and I will grip the two ends with our beaks and soar high into the clouds, carrying you across the peaks to the great lake. But mark this sacred condition: whatever you see below, however high we soar, and whatever mortals may shout from the earth, you must not open your mouth or speak a single syllable! If you speak, you let go of the wood and tumble to your death.'

Shell-Neck swore a solemn oath: 'I swear by the sacred waters that I will keep my jaws clamped like an iron vise. I will not utter a sound, nor even breathe through my mouth, until my feet touch the new lake!'

The two geese fetched a strong branch of sal wood. Shell-Neck clamped his jaws tight across the center, and the two great birds spread their broad white wings, beating the air with powerful strokes. Upward they soared, lifting the heavy tortoise above the dry trees, over the rocky crags, and high into the azure sky.

As they flew over a bustling town, the inhabitants looked up and saw the extraordinary spectacle: two colossal white geese soaring through the heavens carrying a heavy tortoise suspended between their beaks!

Crowds gathered in the streets, pointing and shouting with loud laughter: 'Look! Look at the wonder in the sky! The geese are carrying a round wheel! If that clumsy beast falls, we will roast him in the coals for dinner!'

Hearing the insolent jeers and laughter rising from the ground, Shell-Neck's temper flared with indignant vanity. Forgetting his solemn vow, forgetting the advice of his devoted friends, and forgetting that he was suspended a thousand cubits above the jagged earth, the foolish tortoise opened his jaws to snap: 'Eat the ashes of your own folly, you insolent peasants—'

The instant his jaws parted, the wood slipped from his teeth. Down, down, down tumbled the helpless tortoise through the empty air like a falling stone. He struck the hard flagstones of the town square with a sickening crash, shattering his shell to pieces, and was instantly devoured by the mob.

Hovering in the sky above, Slim and Grim wept for their fallen friend, crying:
"He who neglects the counsel of devoted, prudent friends,
And lets his vanity and wrath achieve his bitter ends,
Shall lose his hold on safety when the mocking voices sound,
And fall like Shell-Neck from the sky to perish on the ground."
moral: He who cannot hold his tongue in the face of mockery destroys himself despite the aid of devoted friends.

title: Forethought Readywit and Fatalist
full_text:
In an expansive, crystal-clear mountain pool fed by perennial springs lived three large, fat carps who had been companions since they were minnows: Anagatavidhata, or Forethought; Pratyutpannamati, or Readywit; and Yadbhavishya, or Fatalist.

One golden evening, as the three friends swam near the surface, several fishermen passed along the grassy bank carrying heavy wicker creels and bamboo spears. Pointing to the water, one fisherman remarked: 'Look at this deep pool! It is teeming with fat, mature fish. We have finished our day's catch on the lower river, but tomorrow morning at daybreak, let us bring our heavy drag-nets here and empty this pool completely!'

Hearing these ominous words, Forethought's fins trembled with alarm. Assembling his two companions, he urged: 'Brothers, you heard the fishermen's threat. When the dawn breaks, they will drag every cubit of this water with their fine-meshed nets. It is madness to remain here a single night. A narrow subterranean canal connects this pool to the deep flowing river half a mile downstream. Let us swim through that passage tonight under the cover of darkness and reach the sanctuary of the great river!'

Readywit replied: 'Forethought speaks with wisdom, but I am reluctant to abandon our ancestral pool before danger actually strikes. If the fishermen arrive with their nets, I will rely upon my quick presence of mind and devise an escape to preserve my life.'

Fatalist, the third fish, laughed scornfully: 'How foolish you both are! What must happen will happen, and what is not destined can never come to pass. If the gods have written in the book of fate that I am to die tomorrow, no subterranean canal can save me; and if I am destined to live, no fisherman's net can harm a scale of my body. Why abandon our comfortable home out of fear of mere words? I will stay right here and accept whatever destiny brings!'

Seeing that his friends refused to heed wise counsel, Forethought swam through the subterranean passage that very midnight, reaching the deep, wide river in safety and freedom.

At dawn, the fishermen arrived with their long drag-nets of woven cord. They waded into the pool from both banks, sweeping the waters from end to end. Every living creature—frogs, turtles, and fish—was trapped in the tightening cords.

As the heavy net was hauled toward the muddy bank, Readywit realized that struggle was futile. Acting with lightning presence of mind, he threw himself upon his back, stiffened his fins, rolled his eyes backward, and remained completely motionless, floating belly-up like a putrefying carcass.

A fisherman seized Readywit by the tail: 'Faugh! This large fish died days ago and has gone rotten!' With a careless flick of his wrist, the fisherman tossed Readywit out of the net into a pool of shallow rainwater near the bank. The instant the man turned his back, Readywit gave a powerful flick of his tail, slipped into the deep reeds, and escaped into the river.

Fatalist, however, relied upon blind fate to save him. When hauled onto the dry sands, he flopped frantically about, gasping and thrashing until a fisherman struck him upon the head with a heavy wooden cudgel, threw him into the wicker basket, and took him to market to be sold.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Forethought prepares his shelter ere the gathering storm-clouds break;
Readywit saves his living breath when perils overtake;
While Fatalist, who trusts to luck and folds his idle fins,
Perishes helplessly in shame where destiny begins."
moral: He who prepares beforehand and he who acts with swift presence of mind survive; but he who relies on blind destiny is ruined.
